title: TB5-13867
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the female principal Appellant), referred herein as the Appellant, XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant's spouse), and XXXX XXXX (a minor and the son of the two adult Appellants), are citizens of Guyana. They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection. The Appellants respectfully request that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and find that they are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellants respectfully request that the RPD refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.

The adult male Appellant and the minor rely on the principal female Appellant's Basis of Claim (BoC) narrative. The principal female Appellant acted as the Designated Representative (DR) for the minor Appellant. Memorandum of Appeal a. What is the applicable standard of review? b. Did the RPD err in finding that there is no nexus between the Appellants' fear and a Convention ground? c. In the alternative, did the RPD err in finding that the Appellants faced a generalized risk in Guyana?
Pursuant to s. 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.
The RAD determines that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The Appellant outlined her family situation in China before she and the male Appellant emigrated to Guyana in 1994 and became citizens. The minor male Appellant was born in Guyana and is a Guyanese citizen.

The adult Appellants became XXXX owners and described how they were robbed, by unknown robbers, on at least four occasions between 2007 and 2014. In each instance, the police were called but gave very little information about the continuing investigation in spite of repeated attempts by the Appellants to acquire this information. The police also demanded payment in order to protect them, saying that the Chinese people always brought trouble. Often when the police came to the XXXX, they XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and did not pay.

As a result of the above, the Appellants felt they were targeted because they were Chinese, much more than businesses owned by native Guyanese. The Appellants submit that the police in Guyana cannot protect Chinese businesses or Chinese people and that there was a lot of corruption among the police in Guyana
The Appellants gave a description of their emigration from Guyana, and the problems they encountered.
The RPD hearing was held on November 17, 2015, and in a decision of November 26, 2015, the RPD found that the Appellants were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

The RPD decision was appealed to the RAD and in a decision of February 17, 2016, the RAD confirmed the RPD decision and found that the Appellants were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

The RAD decision was appealed to the Federal Court, and in a decision of XXXX XXXX, 2016, Justice XXXX allowed the judicial review, setting aside the RAD decision, and remitting it to a differently constituted panel of the RPD for re-determination. Admissibility of Evidence Submitted on Appeal

Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected1 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

It is for the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellant.2 Application of Section 110(4)

Section 110(4) establishes a disjunctive test.3 The RAD must first consider whether the proposed new evidence arose after the rejection of the refugee claims. If it did, the evidence meets the requirements of the section. If it did not, the RAD must consider whether the evidence was reasonably available for presentation to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claims. If it was not reasonably available at that time, it meets the requirements of section 110(4). If the evidence did not arise after the rejection, and it was reasonably available, the RAD must consider whether the Appellant could reasonably have been expected, in their circumstances, to have presented the evidence to the RPD prior to the rejection of their claim. If they could not have been expected to do so, the evidence meets the requirements of the section.

If the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claim, was reasonably available, and could reasonably have been expected, in the circumstances, to be presented to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claim, the evidence does not meet the test in section 110(4). The RAD does not have discretion to admit such evidence.4

As the RAD understands it, section 110(4) provides the Appellant with an opportunity to present evidence that could not have been submitted to the RPD-either because the evidence did not exist at the time of the RPD proceeding, or because it did exist but was unavailable, or because it did exist and was available, but the Appellant could not have been expected to present it to the RPD.

Section 110(4) does not provide an opportunity for the Appellant to complete a deficient record submitted to the RPD; rather, it allows for the correction of errors of fact, errors in law, or mixed errors of fact and law.5

In considering whether the evidence arose after the rejection of the claim, the RAD will not restrict its analysis to the date on the proposed new evidence. In the RAD's view, a document's "newness" cannot be tested solely by the date of its creation; what is important is the event or circumstance sought to be proved by the evidence.6 Old evidence remains old evidence, even if it is placed in a new document with a recent date. Assessment of Evidence that Meets the Requirements of Section 110(4)

Where a document meets the test in section 110(4), as discussed above, the RAD will conduct a further assessment of that evidence. While section 110(4) provides the RAD with factors to consider in assessing a document's "newness," these factors alone cannot determine the admissibility of new evidence in an appeal. To put it simply, if a document is lacking in credibility, or is irrelevant, it would make little sense to admit such a document even if it meets the test in section 110(4).

In Singh,7 the Federal Court of Appeal held that there is no valid reason the RAD cannot apply the criteria set out in Raza8 to the assessment of new evidence. While Raza predates the introduction of the IRPA section 110(4), it is based on the nearly-identical wording of section 113(a). In that case, the Court of Appeal held that new evidence should be considered for its credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality, in addition to any express statutory provisions.9 In Singh, the Court found that the criteria from Raza are necessarily implied in the wording of section 110(4).10

Where evidence meets the test in section 110(4), the RAD will go on to assess it for credibility. While this is a factor set out in Raza, there are also other reasons to apply to it. Section 171(a.3) of the IRPA allows the RAD to "...receive and base a decision on evidence that is adduced in the proceedings and considered credible or trustworthy in the circumstances." This provision makes it clear that, in addition to the factors in section 110(4), the RAD must consider the credibility or trustworthiness of proposed new evidence.

Relevance is a basic condition for the admissibility of any piece of evidence.11 RAD Rule 3(3)(g)(iii) requires the Appellant's Memorandum to include full and detailed submissions about how any proposed new evidence "relates to the Appellant." It would be highly inefficient for the RAD to admit irrelevant evidence, and contrary to section 162(2) of the IRPA, which requires all divisions of the IRB to "...deal with all proceedings before it as informally and quickly as the circumstances and the considerations of fairness and natural justice permit."

In addition to credibility and relevance, the factors in Raza include "newness" and "materiality." Newness is implicitly incorporated into section 110(4) and does not require additional analysis. The Federal Court of Appeal has also found materiality to be redundant, as it is also found in section 110(6) of the IRPA, which describes when the RAD may hold an oral hearing.12

For these reasons, the RAD will apply the following factors to considering the Appellant's proposed new evidence. It will first consider whether the evidence that passes the test in section 110(4). If not, the RAD has no discretion to admit the evidence. If the evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4), the RAD will assess its credibility and relevance in order to determine whether it is admissible.

The Appellant submitted a news article from I News, dated August 25, 2014. This article has been submitted to the RPD, post hearing, but was returned as the RPD had already reached and written its decision. The article in question predates the RPD hearing by over a year, and predates the RAD decision by sixteen months. The RAD finds that this article was available prior to the RPD hearing, and the RAD according to section 110(4) of IRPA, is unable to accept this document in that it was reasonably available at the time of the RPD hearing.

The Appellant supports the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93, as the standard of review for appeals to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica13 provides guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD, to decisions of the first level administrative tribunal.

The Court stated that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard. Pursuant to s. 111(2)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD may refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination if it is "of the opinion" that it cannot make a decision confirming or setting aside the RPD decision without hearing the evidence presented before the RPD. This recognizes that there may be cases where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, because those cases require an assessment of credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears. It further indicates that although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.
Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its assessment of the RPD's decision on the basis of the principles outlined above. Merits of the Appeal Credibility
The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants allegations were credible. Nexus

The RPD referenced the testimony of the female Appellant, where she stated: that she was robbed by different people that she did not know, that there were no specific groups of people she fears, that she could not identify such people and groups, that she feared criminals in general, that she heard of other XXXX being robbed, and that none of the robbers said anything about why they were robbing the XXXX.

In response to counsel's questioning, she testified that she heard about some Chinese acquaintances being robbed but knew little about it. She stated that Chinese people in particular were being targeted for a crime. She also testified that she had not heard other native people making racist remarks, only the police. The female Appellant also stated that she did not know if she would be safe in Guyana if she were not Chinese.

The male Appellant testified that Chinese businesses were targeted, and stated that his opinion was based on local hearsay that Chinese people have money and are soft or weak. He further testified that most robberies are done to Chinese people, and he is aware of this because locals are giving this information.

In spite of counsel's arguments with respect to nexus, the RPD found that the fact that Chinese people are victims of crime does not, in and of itself, mean that Chinese people are disproportionately victimized or that they are targeted because of their race. The RPD found that the male Appellant's testimony simply reflects a subjective belief, and a fragile one at that, and it is based on things he has heard from locals in Guyana. With respect to the articles submitted by the Appellants, and referenced below, the RPD notes that in only one article is there any mention that Chinese people are specifically targeted. The RPD notes this opinion came from an associate of one of the victims who was interviewed by a journalist, and no information was provided as to the basis for this belief. The RPD referenced a Freedom House article that describes some racial polarization in the police between Indo-and Afro-Guyanese and police corruption in general.14

Referencing National Documentation Package (NDP) documentation15, the RPD states that violent crime against everyone is a major problem. Robbery and murder on the rise. The RPD gives figures for robberies in Guyana, indicating that there are an average of three armed robberies per day. The RPD submits that the Appellant's documenting six robberies against Chinese people in a three-year period does not reveal a disproportionate targeting of Chinese people, given that there were probably 3,000 robberies in Guyana during this time. The RPD referred to the Appellant's reference of federal jurisprudence,16 with respect to racial motivation, but finds that the belief of the male Appellant is not supported by evidence.

The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the criminals who targeted the Appellants were motivated by nothing other than money. As a result, there is no nexus to a Convention ground, and the Appellants are not Convention refugees.

The Appellants submit, in spite of their credible allegations, the RPD determined that they were not Convention refugees, because of a lack of nexus to a Convention ground. They submit that the RPD erred in finding that they were not targeted in Guyana because of their Chinese ethnicity, but were merely victims of criminal acts directed at business owners. The Appellant further submits that the RPD failed to properly consider the evidence supporting their well-founded fear of persecution based on their Chinese ethnicity. The Appellants referred to new evidence submitted to the RAD, evidence that was rejected according to section 110(4) of IRPA.

The Appellants submit that objective country wide documentation supports the above submission, albeit there is not a vast amount of objective evidence because the ethnic minorities make up a small portion of the Guyanese population. The Appellants disclosed an article from October 13, 201517 regarding the armed robbery of a Chinese restaurant owner. Citing other documentation, referenced below, the Appellants rejected the RPD's finding that rejects the article because a close associate of the victim made this statement. The Appellants also submit that the RPD failed to consider the balance of the article that outlines further attacks against Chinese nationals.

The Appellants submitted further articles that described how other Chinese nationals are targeted by gunmen.18 They submit that this evidence corroborates their subjective belief that they were targeted because of their Chinese ethnicity.

The Appellants referred to the RPD decision, paragraph 16,19 where it states, "...when protection was sought, the police may have been influenced by racism." They submit that the RPD found this racism to be relevant to the issue of nexus, because it speaks only to the motivations of the police, not the motives for the actual crimes that were carried out against them. The Appellants submit that this finding is unsustainable in law.

The RAD references NDP documentation20 in referring to the racial tension that existed prior to the 2011 elections. The tensions noted, were between the Afro-Guyanese population and the Indo-Guyanese population. The RPD also quoted the United States 2015 Crime in Safety Report that ethnic and religious diversity have not been directly linked to incidents of violence in recent years.21

The RAD references NDP documentation22 to note that the police force is predominantly Afro-Guyanese and that Indo-Guyanese business owners tend to rely on private security providers with their own weapons for protection rather than the police force. The RAD finds, given the NDP documentation, that the security environment for business owners in Guyana is precarious. The documentation referenced state that conflicts have existed primarily between the Afro-Guyanese and Indo-Guyanese. There was no documentation in the articles to suggest that ethnic Chinese were being targeted because of their race. The articles presented seem to focus on the fact that people of perceived wealth or money were targeted. The Appellants are XXXX owners, and would reasonably be perceived as people of wealth or having money.

With respect to the specific robberies testified to by the Appellants, the police, according to the documentation presented,23 visited the scene, interviewed the family, but no useful report was taken. The RPD found the Appellants credible, and stated in its decision, that there may have been some racial motivation by the local police. The RAD cannot agree with this comment in the RPD decision. The RAD finds that the RPD relied upon the testimony of the Appellants, testimony that the RAD finds is speculative. No documentary proof has been provided to support such a conclusion; it relies on the testimony of the Appellants. The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that this testimony is speculative in nature, and is the personal opinion of the Appellants. The RAD prefers the NDP documentation quoted over the personal opinion and speculation of the Appellants.

In order for the issue of race to be engaged as nexus, it must be the motivation for persecution. The RAD finds that there is not sufficient documentary evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities that the risk to ethnic Chinese business owners is heightened in comparison to other business owners. The RAD notes federal jurisprudence to support the finding that the ethnic Chinese are not specifically targeted in Guyana.24 The RAD finds that there was no nexus in this particular case, and that the Appellants are not Convention refugees. Persons in Need of Protection

The RPD found that, under subsection 97(1) of the Act, that the Appellants would not be subjected to a risk personally since they are victims of general crime. They identified no agents of harm other than common criminals and testified they fear only common criminals. They have not established a motive for the robberies other than money. The RPD found that any harm they would face in the future would be crimes for which they are not personally targeted. As a result, he found the Appellants were not persons in need of protection.
The Appellants did not specifically address this issue on appeal.

The RAD reviewing the documentation and testimony at the hearing, finds, on a balance of probabilities, that there was no evidence that the Appellants were targeted personally. The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that they were targeted because they were XXXX owners and perceived to be wealthy and/or have money. In the alternative-Generalized Risk

In the alternative, the RPD found that the Appellants are also disqualified under the "generalized risk" clause in sub-paragraph 97(1)(b)(ii) of the Act. The RPD stated that risk may only lead to refugee protection if, "the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country."

The RPD reasoned that the Appellants risk is that of being robbed or burglarized in the context of a common crime targeting business owners and people of money. The RPD stated there is no agent of persecution identified other than common criminals, and there is no indication of escalating harm, repeat victimization by anyone, or risk of future reprisals.

The RPD next decided the risk faced by the Appellants was faced by the population generally, or even a significant group of the population. In the RPD's view, business owners and people with money are a significant group within the population. As found above, robberies in Guyana are common and widespread, and the RPD rejected the submission that the Appellants were in any way personally targeted. The RPD pointed out that in this particular case, there is no indication that the Appellants had been or would be singled out among other business owners for repeat victimization.

The RPD found, pursuant to subparagraph 97(1)(b)(ii) of the Act that the risk faced by the Appellants is a risk faced generally by other individuals in Guyana. The RPD found that the Appellants are therefore not persons in need of protection.

The Appellants submit that the RPD failed to appreciate that the risk faced by the Appellants sufficiently particularized such that they are not excluded from the definition of, "persons in need of protection." According to the Appellants, the critical factor is the risk they face is personalized because of the racism of the police. They further submit that the risk faced by the Appellants submits that the Chinese is distinctly different from the general risks faced by all Guyana.

The Appellants quoted federal jurisprudence to submit that the fact that because the risk that they face has its genesis in criminal activity does not in itself mean that the risk is one generally faced by others in Guyana.25 The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in finding that they face a generalized risk in Guyana.

The RAD notes, quoting NDP documentation,26 that violent crimes continue to rise, and that there is no indication in the sources that the risk is higher for ethnic Chinese people. The fact that a person or group of people may be victimized repeatedly or more frequently by criminals, for example, because of their perceived wealth or because they live in a more dangerous area,27 or that they continue to be pursued after reporting to police or relocating (Rodriguez Perez),28 or that they face retaliation for not complying with the demands of the criminals,29 does not remove the risk from the exception if it is one faced generally by others. Thus, the consequential harm faced in these circumstances does not mean that the risk is not a generalized one.30

The RAD concurs with the RPD that this claim would fall under the category of "generalized" risk for the following reasons. The RAD finds that the Appellants were not personally targeted, their lives are not at risk, and the risk is one that is generally faced by others in Guyana i.e. individuals perceived to be wealthy or have money. The Appellant and her husband were business owners, and the documentation quoted above clearly indicates that business owners are targeted by criminals in Guyana. The RAD considered the NDP documentation quoted by the RPD, and finds that serious crimes, including murder and armed robbery are common. The documentation also states that robberies occur regularly especially in businesses and shopping districts and that they are becoming increasingly common. The RAD also found nothing in the documentation submitted or testimony, to indicate that these robberies are personally motivated against the Appellants or by ethnicity, but rather are criminal acts against individuals perceived to have money. Disposition

The RAD finds that the Appellants are not Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection, and dismisses the appeal, and confirms the RPD's decision according to section 111(1)(a) of IRPA.
